content_voiceover: This slide profiles adult T-cell leukemia lymphoma clinically and immunophenotypically. It's a disease of older adults, median age around sixty, with striking geographic clustering in southern Japan and northeastern Taiwan, both HTLV-1 endemic regions. HTLV-1 is transmitted through breastfeeding, blood products, and sexual contact; the carrier rate in Taiwan is under one percent, and only about two and a half percent of HTLV-1 carriers ever progress to ATLL, reflecting a long latency and multistep leukemogenesis. Clinically, patients present with leukocytosis, skin rash, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and hypercalcemia, that last finding from PTHrP production is a classic board pearl. Morphologically the tumor cells are medium to large with markedly polylobated nuclei, the so-called flower cells, seen in the image. Immunophenotypically, the normal counterpart is the regulatory T cell, so ATLL is CD4 positive, CD25 positive, CD2, CD3, and CD5 positive, but CD7 and CD8 negative, and it usually shows loss of CD7 expression, a useful discriminator. Because the neoplastic cells are essentially regulatory T cells, patients develop profound immunosuppression and are prone to opportunistic infections, which often drive mortality more than the leukemia itself.
keypoints: Endemic to southern Japan and northeastern Taiwan; caused by HTLV-1
Only ~2.5% of HTLV-1 carriers ever develop ATLL
Classic tetrad: leukocytosis, skin rash, lymphadenopathy, hypercalcemia (PTHrP)
Flower cells = polylobated tumor cells; normal counterpart is regulatory T cell
Immunophenotype CD4+/CD25+ but CD7-, causing poor immunity and opportunistic infection
keypoint_voiceover: Remember ATLL as HTLV-1 plus Treg plus hypercalcemia. It's endemic to southern Japan and northeastern Taiwan, driven by HTLV-1, though only about two and a half percent of carriers ever develop the leukemia. The tumor cell mimics a regulatory T cell, CD4 positive, CD25 positive, but CD7 negative, and the polylobated flower cell on blood smear plus hypercalcemia from PTHrP are the two highest-yield exam clues.
